source.title: On the Origin of Algorithmic Progress in AI
source.authors: Hans Gundlach; Alex Fogelson; Jayson Lynch; A. Trišović; Jonathan Rosenfeld; A. Sandhu; Neil C. Thompson

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs its own language-model scaling experiments and analyzes compute-allocation curves, using validation loss and compute-equivalent gains to examine power-law scaling and how scaling depends on architecture and allocation.
record.gate_note: The small-model scaling experiments and the Kaplan-versus-Chinchilla allocation analysis bear on the claim. The single-scale algorithm ablations in Section 3 and literature estimates are not rows: they do not directly report the scaling behavior named by the claim. The study does not test architecture shape at fixed parameter count, other modalities or regimes, or downstream-task predictability.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out pretraining loss across compute scales and compares fitted scaling exponents across architectures and optimizers. Its allocation analysis derives consequences of assumed scaling laws rather than independently testing compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that algorithmic efficiency gains depend strongly on compute scale and reference algorithm. Their small-scale experiments find architecture-dependent exponents but little exponent change for the tested Transformer component bundle and optimizers. Large frontier gains are extrapolated or analytically derived, rather than measured in frontier training runs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses small C4-trained LSTM and Transformer sweeps, fixed token-to-parameter ratios, and compute-equivalent comparisons rather than reproducing the original large-scale parameter/token scaling experiments. It also analyzes Kaplan-to-Chinchilla rebalancing analytically.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes the scaling exponent: LSTM versus Modern Transformer differs, while Modern versus Retro Transformer is reported as nearly identical. The LSTM-to-Transformer efficiency gap also depends on the loss threshold. The Kaplan-to-Chinchilla efficiency gap changes with compute. SGD and AdamW show little scaling difference, although SGD is described as less stable.

fits_no_version.finding: R8–R9 reconstruct published allocation prescriptions and minimize an assumed loss function.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Assuming the Chinchilla loss function determines an analytical optimal allocation against which Kaplan prescriptions can be compared.

fits_no_version.finding: R10–R12 quantify conditional compute-equivalent gains from rebalancing allocations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under assumed Chinchilla ground truth, the efficiency benefit of replacing Kaplan allocation depends on the target compute scale.

record.problems: The experimental models are small and the authors describe the study as non-exhaustive. They do not run dataset ablations, and they note that more extensive hyperparameter searches, especially for LSTMs, could change the results. The Kaplan-to-Chinchilla analysis assumes Chinchilla-optimal loss as ground truth. Numerical scaling-fit uncertainties are not reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Section 3's fixed-size algorithm ablation results are excluded because they do not report scaling behavior for the claim. Literature-only estimates in Sections 3.3 and 6 are also excluded as they are not results from this study's own experiments.

untested.parts: Independent parameter and token sweeps with other resources non-bottlenecked, and extension to large models. The supplied text does not numerically establish the full compute span of the fitted experimental frontier.
No predictions from small-run fits are checked against independently trained runs orders of magnitude larger; frontier estimates are extrapolations.
No independent test of loss-minimizing parameter/token allocations or their stability across compute budgets. The analytical allocation results assume the Chinchilla loss model.
No controlled loss comparison across a wide range of depths, widths, and architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Downstream performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Controlled sensitivity to parameter counting, datasets, fitting methods, and training schedules individually. Explanations of the original Kaplan–Chinchilla disagreement are cited from other studies.

missing.what: Add the study's numerical Modern Transformer compute-scaling exponent, 0.094, to R1.

Record that fitting L=E+AC^(-α), with E constrained to 1.3–2.2, yields irreducible loss near 1.9 for Modern Transformer, Retro Transformer, and LSTM. This supplies the basis for the offset used in their power-law comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Different architecture-specific exponents do not limit V1, which asserts power-law form rather than exponent universality. The allocation calculations cannot independently validate assumptions from the original scaling studies. Numerical fit uncertainties and quantitative goodness-of-fit statistics are not reported in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments fit validation loss along compute-frontier runs with a fixed token-to-parameter ratio; they do not independently sweep parameters and tokens while holding compute or the other quantities non-bottlenecked, and the experimental models are small.
The paper extrapolates measured scaling behavior to frontier compute but does not test predictions from small-run fits against runs orders of magnitude larger.

The paper gives an analytical comparison of Kaplan and Chinchilla allocations, assuming Chinchilla-optimal loss as ground truth; it does not experimentally optimize parameter and token counts across compute budgets.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer settings are tested.

The study examines architecture-dependent scaling and the Kaplan-to-Chinchilla allocation comparison, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, fitting procedures, datasets, and training schedules.

rows.subject: Modern Transformer
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 29M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Scaled hidden dimension from 32 to 256 and fit a power law to Pareto-optimal points.
rows.value: figure only; the authors fit a power law to the frontier points
rows.note: The text states that the authors fit a power law; numerical fit parameters are not given in the text.
rows.check: The fitted quantity is validation loss minus an estimated irreducible loss of 1.9. Section 6.3 reports a Transformer scaling exponent of 0.094, so the result is not entirely figure-only.

rows.subject: LSTM
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 11.2M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Scaled hidden dimension from 32 to 256 and fit a power law to Pareto-optimal points.
rows.value: figure only; the authors fit a power law to the frontier points
rows.note: The text states that the authors fit a power law; numerical fit parameters are not given in the text.
rows.check: Specify that the power-law fit uses validation loss minus 1.9. Numerical LSTM fit parameters and fit uncertainties are unavailable in the supplied text.

rows.subject: Retro Transformer
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 29M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared its scaling curve with the Modern Transformer after reverting four algorithmic components.
rows.note: The text explicitly characterizes the scaling difference as minimal.
rows.check: This row measures exponent sensitivity to component changes, rather than power-law form itself. The reported exponent difference is minimal, so observed is incorrect for setup dependence.

rows.subject: Modern Transformer
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 29M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared the fitted loss-scaling curve with the LSTM curve.
rows.value: significantly different scaling exponents; the authors describe increasing returns to scale; figure only
rows.note: The result is a direct architecture-dependent difference in scaling behavior.
rows.check: Different exponents support architecture dependence, but do not qualify or contradict V1, which does not require a common exponent across architectures. Statistical significance is not established by reported uncertainties.

rows.subject: Modern Transformer
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 29M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute needed to reach the stated loss threshold against the LSTM.
rows.measure: Compute-efficiency ratio at a fixed loss threshold
rows.note: This is a fixed-threshold comparison, not a direct numerical report of the fitted exponents.
rows.check: This threshold-specific efficiency ratio bears on scaling dependence jointly with R6; alone it does not establish a power law or exponent dependence. The 6.28× value at loss 5.3 comes from scaling fits, not simply fixed-size training curves.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2 reports 6.28× at loss 5.3; Section 4.1.2 repeats the comparison.

rows.subject: Modern Transformer
rows.size_stated: 1.6M to 29M parameters across the scaling runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute needed to reach the stated validation-loss threshold against the LSTM.
rows.measure: Compute-efficiency ratio at a fixed validation-loss threshold
rows.note: The gap differs substantially from the 6.28× result at the higher loss threshold.
rows.check: Together with R5, the larger efficiency gap at lower loss corroborates architecture-dependent scaling. It does not independently measure V1's power-law form.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.2 reports the 26× gap at validation loss 4.4.

rows.subject: Transformer trained with SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared scaling behavior with the Modern Transformer trained using AdamW.
rows.value: little scaling difference; SGD runs were notably more unstable and had slight early concavity
rows.note: The reported scaling difference is small, although training stability differed.
rows.check: The state correctly describes negligible optimizer dependence of the exponent. It must not be read as absence of power-law loss scaling; instability is a separate finding.

rows.subject: Kaplan scaling recommendation
rows.operation_detail: Derived compute-dependent parameter and dataset allocations from the Kaplan recommendations.
rows.note: The paper presents these as the inferred Kaplan scaling recommendations.
rows.check: These are Kaplan prescriptions reconstructed from the original source, serving as analytical inputs. They are not new evidence that these allocations minimize loss.

rows.subject: Chinchilla scaling recommendation
rows.operation_detail: Derived compute-dependent parameter and dataset allocations using the Chinchilla-optimal form.
rows.value: N exponent β/(α+β); D exponent α/(α+β); the paper states parameters and data scale equally
rows.note: The allocation follows the Chinchilla form assumed by the authors for their analysis.
rows.check: Optimal allocation is derived from an assumed Chinchilla loss function, not independently validated. With α=0.34 and β=0.28, the stated formulas give parameter and token exponents approximately 0.452 and 0.548, respectively; they are not exactly equal.

rows.subject: Kaplan scaling recommendation
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss under Kaplan allocation with the Chinchilla-optimal allocation at the same compute.
rows.measure: Compute-equivalent gain from rebalancing to Chinchilla allocation
rows.value: gains remain below 10× for much of the stated compute range
rows.note: The paper says the gap first converges and then diverges as compute grows.
rows.check: A derived efficiency multiplier below 10× does not measure whether optimal allocations follow stable powers or whether fitted exponents depend on setup. Partial has no basis in either version.

rows.subject: Kaplan scaling recommendation
rows.operation_detail: Compared Kaplan allocation with Chinchilla rebalancing at the stated frontier compute.
rows.note: The estimate is part of the paper's extrapolation to the 2023 frontier.
rows.check: The 3.7× value is a conditional analytical estimate at one compute budget, not an allocation or exponent test.

rows.subject: Kaplan scaling recommendation
rows.operation_detail: Compared Kaplan allocation with Chinchilla rebalancing at the stated frontier compute.
rows.note: The estimate is given for the authors' 2025 compute frontier.
rows.check: The nearly 10× value is a conditional analytical estimate at one compute budget. Its listed abstract locator is incorrect: the supplied abstract does not report this value.

rows.subject: Kaplan-to-Chinchilla allocation comparison
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed the compute-equivalent gain function between Kaplan and Chinchilla allocation curves.
rows.measure: Shape of compute-equivalent gain across compute
rows.value: the efficiency gap first converges, then diverges at larger scales
rows.note: This is a scale-dependent change in the relative efficiency curve.
rows.check: Retain only as conditional analytical evidence for bending curves. Substituting Kaplan allocations into the assumed Chinchilla loss yields a sum of different powers, rather than a single power. This does not independently establish fitting-choice dependence or test V3.
